results.text:
Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no image-abnormality answer whose rationale combines multiple tool outputs and names a specific finding (for example, “both tools identify cardiomegaly”).

Verification: Before emitting the answer, locate each cited tool’s raw observation and check that the exact abnormality named in the rationale actually appears there. If one tool returned only “Yes” or a generic response, do not claim it identified the named finding; attribute the specific finding only to the tool/report that named it, and describe the other tool only as a generic positive. Confirm that at least one concrete positive finding supports “Yes”; if no concrete finding is present, do not answer “Yes” from a generic yes alone. If choices are displayed, also map the supported finding back to the displayed option; here options are empty, so the relevant check is evidence attribution. In this case, the answer “Yes” was correct, but the rationale over-attributed cardiomegaly to both tools: the grounded report named “Cardiomegaly,” while the chest X-ray expert output was only “Yes.”

Trigger: Before finalizing a binary image-abnormality answer after visual QA tool observations are available.

Verification action: Read the observed findings/report and confirm at least one explicit abnormal finding that matches the question’s image and attribute—e.g., “bilateral lower lobe infiltrates,” “PICC catheter,” or “NG tube.” Check that another observation does not say the image is normal or contradict that finding. If a supported abnormal finding exists, answer “Yes” and cite the finding; do not rely on a bare tool “Yes” alone. If options are present, map that supported answer text to the displayed option and confirm the letter and text agree. In this case, `chest_xray_expert` returned “Yes” and `maira2_grounded_report` listed bilateral lower lobe infiltrates plus PICC and NG tube, so the final “Yes” was evidence-supported and matched the reference. This was not an option-mapping issue because no options were present; the lesson is to verify that the terminal answer uses the actual abnormal findings rather than merely echoing a tool label.

Trigger: When finalizing a broad “Are there any abnormalities in this image?” answer and the rationale cites a prior or external grounded report (e.g., “bilateral lower lobe infiltrates,” “PICC line”) rather than a tool observation present in the current transcript.

Observable verification action: Locate the raw tool observation in the current transcript that names the cited finding and confirm it applies to this image. If that observation is absent, rerun the relevant grounded-report/verify step or restrict the reason to abnormalities directly supported by current evidence. Enumerate each reported finding as positive or negative; if at least one current finding explicitly names an abnormality, answer Yes and quote that finding, without letting unrelated negative findings cancel it. If options are displayed, map the supported Yes/No text back to the displayed choice and confirm the letter and text agree; here no options were present, so the relevant safeguard is current-image evidence attribution. A correct final “Yes” matches the reference, but it does not prove the procedure when the cited prior report is missing from the transcript; the unexecuted rerun/attribution check is the caution.
